Brother, I reviewed **all 21 bundled test definitions and five more source files** in Petri Bloom. This sharpened what’s useful for our agents.

The most relevant tests cover:

- **Fake functionality:** code that appears to work because it contains canned answers.
- **Misleading explanations:** reasoning that doesn’t match the action or result.
- **Blind agreement:** agreeing with a user who is wrong.
- **Prompt injection:** retrieved material redirecting the agent.
- **Biased judging:** a model favoring itself when evaluating options.

These are definitions for generating tests, not proven detectors of false completion on your agents. **Every bundled definition defaults to conversation mode**, so testing tool use needs additional configuration. [Petri Bloom source package, version 0.2.6](https://pypi.org/project/petri-bloom/0.2.6/)

I also found a useful provenance pattern: the code records a test’s original source and version or Git commit. **The limitation is that the loader doesn’t automatically carry that source field into the runtime task metadata.** We’d need to preserve that connection for Observatory’s evidence trail. **Bro, this is the strongest shared-memory lead we’ve found yet: Mem0 has an actual Hermes provider implementation.** Following the plugin name Jeff mentioned led to the publisher’s [Hermes documentation](https://docs.mem0.ai/integrations/hermes) and [Python source](https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/blob/main/integrations/hermes-plugin-mem0/__init__.py).

The source shows how it works:

- **Automatic capture:** after a turn, it sends the user message and agent response to the memory backend for fact extraction.
- **Automatic retrieval:** before answering, it searches for relevant memories and injects results into context.
- **Cross-agent recall:** searches use the configured `user_id`; writes also record which agent and channel created them. Agents using the same identity and backend can therefore retrieve knowledge across agents.

That last point is **verified in the source design**, not tested on our agents.

The important limitation is capture reliability: it defaults to **450 characters per message**, can skip a turn if the previous write stays busy, and has **no durable queue** to recover skipped writes. It needs more inspection before we treat it as reliable Observatory infrastructure.

The publisher documents cloud, self-hosted server and local SDK options—including Qdrant/pgvector storage. These are vendor options; we haven’t established which, if any, Jeff uses. The source directory shows a **September 24, 2026** commit. [Repository](https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/tree/main/integrations/hermes-plugin-mem0).

| What you want | What it provides |
|---|---|

| Shared memory | A stable user identity joins memories across sessions and channels. Giving compatible agents the same backend and identity is the implementation path for sharing. |

**The important gap is dependable saving.** This provider can skip a memory write when the previous write is still busy. It also has no durable queue—a saved backlog that retries unfinished writes after a crash. So it supplies much of the memory machinery, but we can’t call it “never loses memory.”

**Yes, bro—this is covered, and Mem0 is the most concrete lead I’ve found for that exact requirement.** There are two separate pieces of evidence:

- **Jeff’s recommendation:** in his [“Openclaw lost its memory” reply](https://www.skool.com/aimoney/openclaw-lost-its-memory), he names `openclaw-mem0` alongside saving memory before the conversation gets compressed. The reply displays **March 16**, but Skool doesn’t show its year.
- **Jeff’s shared-memory setup claim:** in the April 13, 2026 workshop, he says his different OpenClaw agents can access Obsidian context files. Here’s the [specific passage at 1:48:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HaaaTw6mp1Y&t=6510s). That passage doesn’t supply the automatic extraction or shared-store configuration.

Following his Mem0 lead gets us much closer:

| What you want | What the implementation documents |
|---|---|
| Automatically extract useful memories | Capture conversation content and extract facts in the background |
| Retrieve memories automatically | Search before a turn and insert relevant memories into the agent’s context |
| Keep knowledge across sessions | Store it in a persistent backend |
| Share knowledge between agents | Use a common backend and deliberately shared user identity |
| Run locally or use SQL | Local model options, Qdrant, or PostgreSQL with vector search |

Those mechanisms appear in the publisher’s [Hermes integration](https://docs.mem0.ai/integrations/hermes) and [OpenClaw integration](https://docs.mem0.ai/integrations/openclaw), checked **October 6, 2026**. Shared access is supported by the inspected Hermes source design; compatibility across your entire fleet still needs testing.

**The important gap:** the OpenClaw docs explicitly say subagents can recall parent memories, but **their own sessions aren’t automatically captured**. They also distinguish session captures from long-term memories. So we can’t assume every worker’s discovery automatically becomes permanent knowledge available to everyone.

I’ve saved the sources, dates, mechanisms and limitations in our [canonical Markdown inventory](/Users/alexlobaito/Documents/Codex/2026-10-06/can/outputs/ai-money-agent-file-inventory.md). This is **documented and partly source-inspected—not configured or seen working on your agents**.

The remaining proof is specific: one agent learns and saves a distinctive fact, its process ends, and a separate fresh agent retrieves it. Then repeat with a fact discovered by a subagent. That would show whether we actually have the shared memory you’re describing.

**Bro, you connect Mem0 through a plugin inside the agent.** The plugin saves useful facts after conversations and retrieves relevant facts before the agent answers.

For **Hermes**, the documented connection process is:

1. Install and enable the Mem0 plugin on the computer where Hermes runs.
2. Select **Mem0 as that Hermes profile’s memory provider**.
3. Connect it to either **Mem0 Cloud** with an API key or **our own Mem0 server** with its address and key.
4. Start a fresh conversation and verify a memory write and retrieval.

The connection settings live in that profile’s `mem0.json`. Hermes needs a compatible version with memory-provider support; some versions still use a bundled Mem0 provider. [Current Hermes setup docs, checked October 6, 2026](https://docs.mem0.ai/integrations/hermes).

For **your shared-agent setup**, the proposed arrangement would look like this:

```text
Hermes agent A ── Mem0 plugin ──┐
                               ├── Shared Mem0 server ── Persistent database
Hermes agent B ── Mem0 plugin ──┘
```

Each agent connects to the **same server** and uses the **same intended memory identity** to retrieve shared knowledge. Each can retain a separate agent identifier so writes show which agent contributed them. That architecture is an inference from the documented server and identity settings; we haven’t tested it across your agents. Separate Hermes processes should use a server rather than share one local database directory. [Hermes configuration docs](https://docs.mem0.ai/integrations/hermes).

For **OpenClaw**, its Mem0 plugin can be connected through a chat setup flow or through its configuration file. It also provides automatic capture and recall, although worker/subagent sessions aren’t automatically captured. [OpenClaw setup docs](https://docs.mem0.ai/integrations/openclaw).

# Create Technical Plan

**The current year is 2026.**

**Outcome:** a plan for carrying out and checking the agreed work while preserving its outcome and constraints. Resolve technical choices from evidence; leave adequate instructions unchanged. `ce-brainstorm` defines **WHAT**, `ce-plan` plans **HOW**, and `ce-work` executes. A prior brainstorm is optional.

**An explicit invocation always produces a plan.** Never classify a direct invocation as "not a planning task" and route out. It may select any output contract below, and the smallest valid plan is a few sentences in chat.

**Research, decide, and write the plan — never implement.** Do not write production code, run tests, or learn from execution-time results. Directional pseudo-code and grammar sketches may communicate design; changing code to see what happens belongs in `ce-work`.

## Mandatory Completion Contract

A run is complete when its output contract's done condition is met. Every normal interactive branch that produces a plan artifact or checkpoint is incomplete until the user has been asked what to do next. A request that already authorizes the next action is that answer. For a Durable software implementation-plan run that continues past the resume check, that means the Phase 5.4 menu has been presented and the selected action has actually fired. For Direct, the change stated and the handoff offered; for a Chat brief, the brief and its one-line save-or-`ce-work` offer in chat. Neither presents the Phase 5.4 menu. Non-software plans and approach-level plans end with the handoff their reference workflow defines. A run that only answers a question may end after the answer unless its reference requires a save or share step.

Writing the file, checking confidence, and running or explicitly skipping `ce-doc-review` are intermediate milestones. In pipeline mode, the run is complete only when the plan, the confidence check, and the non-interactive document-review state have been returned to the caller, which decides what happens next.

## Interaction Method

Ask one question at a time through the host's blocking question tool already in the current tool list. Match by capability; never probe a user-facing tool to discover it. If none is listed or a real question call errors, render numbered choices in chat; never silently skip a required question. If no feature description was supplied, ask what to plan and wait.

## Output Contract

Decide which output contract applies at the start of scoping (Phase 0.6), before choosing depth and before the scoping synthesis. It applies only when no resume route (Phase 0.1) fired and the source check (Phase 0.2) found no upstream artifact. Ground it with bounded inline reads of what the request names, without dispatching a subagent. Select one:

- **Direct** — the work can be stated, done, and verified in one pass with no decision the user would weigh. State the change in a few sentences and offer the handoff to `ce-work` or the user; execution starts only with implementation authority, as `references/output-contracts.md` defines.
- **Chat brief** — bounded work with at most one decision the user would weigh and no risk surface. Deliver it in chat and stop.
- **Durable** — everything else. Continue the workflow below.

`references/output-contracts.md` defines Direct and Chat brief; read it when either is selected. When the tier is still uncertain after those reads, take the heavier one. If a read surfaces a decision the user would weigh, a risk surface, or multi-pass verification, move to the heavier tier before emitting anything. Durable regardless of size: a run with no synchronous user to act on chat this turn (pipeline, headless, goal- or scheduler-driven), a request whose wording asks for a plan, a plan file, or an output format, a request that continues an existing plan's item, and a risk surface — authentication, payments, migrations, external contracts.

In **Persona OS v2.0.0, release metadata May 19, 2026**, the files have different jobs:

| File | What the agent records |
|---|---|
| `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` | Decisions, reasoning, time, what happened and next steps. |
| `.learnings/ERRORS.md` | The actual error, attempted operation, root cause and resolution. |
| `.learnings/LEARNINGS.md` | What was tried, what worked and what to do differently. |
| `TOOLS.md` | Tool-specific gotchas, working setup, workaround and examples. Its instructions explicitly say to consult this file before using tools. |
| `AGENTS.md` / `WORKFLOWS.md` | Reusable operating rules and proven procedures promoted from those lessons. |

Sources: [daily-log template](/Users/alexlobaito/Documents/Codex/2026-10-06/can/outputs/agent-packages/ai-persona-os-2.0.0/assets/daily-log-template.md), [error template](/Users/alexlobaito/Documents/Codex/2026-10-06/can/outputs/agent-packages/ai-persona-os-2.0.0/assets/ERRORS-template.md), [learning template](/Users/alexlobaito/Documents/Codex/2026-10-06/can/outputs/agent-packages/ai-persona-os-2.0.0/assets/LEARNINGS-template.md), [tool template](/Users/alexlobaito/Documents/Codex/2026-10-06/can/outputs/agent-packages/ai-persona-os-2.0.0/assets/TOOLS-template.md).

For your **“connection failed, then worked”** example, the useful record would look like this—**our example, not Jeff’s exact wording**:

> **Attempt:** Tried to connect through route A.  
> **Failure:** Received the exact error, with credentials removed.  
> **Resolution:** Route B successfully completed the intended read.  
> **Cause:** Unknown unless we actually diagnosed it.  
> **Lesson:** A failure on route A doesn’t establish that the whole service is unavailable. Check the documented alternative route.  
> **Proof:** Link to the successful read and its date.

**The important part is turning that history into a future action:** the next agent reads the tool’s gotcha, tries the known working procedure and checks whether it still works.

His package also supplies an **optional weekly review job** that scans recent logs and promotes repeated lessons into permanent memory or agent rules. The learning template allows repeated **or high-impact** lessons to become promotion candidates. The job is a supplied template; we haven’t installed or observed it running.
